stories.summary: By the 1990s Indian cotton was being ravaged by bollworms, and farmers were stuck in an escalating race of ever more pesticide. Genetically modified BT cotton, which bollworms don't attack, was available around the world, but the Indian government invoked the precautionary principle and banned all GM crops. Farmers in Gujarat got BT seed through the black market and planted it anyway. In 2002 cotton failed across Gujarat, except on the BT farms. The government's response was to declare the only surviving crops illegal and order them destroyed. Sharad Joshi's Shetkari Sanghatana gathered farmers from Maharashtra and elsewhere, marched to Gujarat, stood on those fields and said 'over our dead bodies', then marched to Delhi with bales of cotton. Barun Mitra spoke at the press conference. The Vajpayee government relented and lifted the ban. When Amit last checked, over 90% of India's cotton was BT and India had passed China as the world's biggest cotton producer and exporter. The sequel: India stalled at two generations of GM cotton while the world moved further ahead, so farmers turned to the black market again for HTBT cotton, and some were arrested for it.
stories.insight: Farmers are often talked about as if they have no agency, yet here they saved themselves by defying the state out of plain self-interest. Satyagraha is not only a pre-Independence word. One of independent India's most inspiring campaigns of civil disobedience was fought for the freedom to plant a better seed.
stories.quote: So get this, it's a catastrophe. Cotton farms everywhere have failed. Bollworms have finally gotten too much. But all the BT cotton people, that cotton has grown. So guess what the government did? The government said, Hey, that's illegal. We're going to destroy those crops.

stories.topic: Sharad Joshi: From Bern to a Farm in Ambethan
stories.summary: Sharad Joshi was born on 3 September 1935 and studied commerce at Sydenham College. He taught economics and statistics around 1957, then became a civil servant, and from 1968 to 1977 worked in informatics in Bern, Switzerland, and with the UN. In 1977, in his forties, he came back to India, bought 23 acres in Ambethan village in Pune district and became a full-time farmer. He soon saw that everything was broken. He looked past the usual answer of government handouts and traced the problem to state overreach. He also rejected the pessimism that such ideas are too counterintuitive for ordinary people. He built the Shetkari Sanghatana, drew lakhs of farmers to his rallies, and coined phrases like 'negative subsidy'. He also saw a point Mrinal Pande later made in a Pragati symposium Amit edited: behind every Indian crisis lies a further crisis of the women in it. So around the mid-1980s he founded the women's wing Shetkari Mahila Aghadi, whose legendary rally drew two lakh women farmers and no men. Later he spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where nobody listened.
stories.insight: Amit's answer to the lament that independent India produced no great leaders is that it did, and we didn't pay attention. Joshi showed that liberal economic ideas can become mass politics. He did not dilute the diagnosis; he trusted farmers to recognise it from their own lives.
stories.quote: Sharad Joshi was not bound by such pessimism. He said that no, this is something every farmer should understand intuitively.

stories.topic: The Farmers Who Had Lived Hayek
stories.summary: About five or six years before this recording, Barun Mitra took Amit to a gathering near Nashik where farmer leaders from across Maharashtra, including Shetkari Sanghatana people, were meeting. The visit produced Amit's only Hindi episode of The Seen and the Unseen, with Gunvant Patil. What moved Amit was a contrast. His own beliefs about liberty and the parasitic state came from books and frameworks, at a distance. Farmer after farmer there held exactly the same beliefs, but had reached them through lived experience.
stories.insight: Grassroots politics need not be only populism and handouts. People can see and clearly describe what is being done to them. The idea that farmers can't understand markets is the real condescension.
stories.quote: They had not read Hayek and Bastiat, but they agreed with every word that Bastiat or Hayek would have written because it was a lived experience.

stories.summary: To show what an APMC means to a farmer, Amit applies it to his own trade. Imagine a 'CPMC' for columnists: he and Ajay could legally sell their columns to only one central party. It would pay them perhaps a tenth of what they earn now, anyone who wanted the column would pay a crazy markup, and the whole thing would run on committee politics. No city dweller would tolerate being told to buy groceries from one place at twenty times the price. Yet comfortable urban elites dismiss freeing farmers with 'farmers will get exploited', even though the recent farm bills left APMCs in place and only added the choice to sell elsewhere.
stories.insight: Apply a restriction to your own life and its absurdity becomes obvious. The loudest defenders of 'protecting' farmers usually enjoy the very freedoms they would deny them.
stories.quote: No one's telling me that I can buy my grocery only from one place and at twenty x a price I would otherwise have.

stories.topic: From Punjab's Paddy Fields to Delhi's Smog
stories.summary: Punjab is relatively arid and has limited groundwater, so it should not be growing water-hungry rice. But the state guarantees an MSP for rice and gives farmers free electricity. Farmers use that electricity to run bore wells and tube wells, pump out far more groundwater than the ecosystem can bear, and grow rice. After the harvest, the cheapest way to clear the stubble is to burn it, and the wind carries the smoke to Delhi in its worst smog months. No Delhi chief minister can fix this, because the cause lies outside his jurisdiction. Ajay totals up the damage. Each rupee raised in taxes costs society roughly three rupees in GDP. That money subsidises rice and wheat in Punjab and Haryana, and the cheap grain harms people's health, drains groundwater, strains the electricity system and fills the Hindi heartland's air with particulate matter. Amit adds that during Tamil Nadu's water crisis, social media urged people to take bucket baths instead of showers, while most of the water was going to crops that should never have been grown there.
stories.insight: One well-meant subsidy can spread into groundwater collapse, a diabetes-friendly diet and a capital city's air. The costs of a policy often land far away from where it was made, on people who had no say in it.
stories.quote: And it's politically almost impossible to solve because what is a Delhi chief minister to do when the problem is caused by farmers in Punjab over which he has no jurisdiction?

recommendations.item: Down to Earth
recommendations.creator: Sharad Joshi
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation, held up on camera. It is a collection of Joshi's columns.
recommendations.reason: Joshi was a great thinker and politician who also took the role of public intellectual seriously and worked hard to get his thinking out. If you want to understand agriculture from the view of a farmer who lived it and led a great farmers' movement, this is the book to read.

recommendations.item: Talking to an Empty Room
recommendations.creator: Sharad Joshi
recommendations.context: Amit's second recommendation, a collection of Joshi's speeches in the Rajya Sabha.
recommendations.reason: The title breaks Amit's heart. Joshi spent years in Parliament with great ideas that nobody paid attention to, and the country would have gained a lot by listening.

recommendations.item: The Wizard and the Prophet
recommendations.creator: Charles C Mann
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, about Norman Borlaug and William Vogt (Amit helped with the pronunciation of Vogt).
recommendations.reason: It covers the tension between the scientific and industrial revolution in agriculture and concerns about sustainability. Ajay calls this the great food-system question of the next 25 years: how to feed 1.4 billion people sustainably, in a way that also fits with public health.

recommendations.item: The Mystery of Capital
recommendations.creator: Hernando De Soto
recommendations.context: An unplanned 'random reco' in the middle of the land discussion, while Amit explains why farmers can't raise credit on their land.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it one of the greatest books he has read, one that opened his mind about economics and gave him many 'today I learned' moments. Its key idea is 'dead capital': assets such as untitled slum homes or land with restricted use that are worth something but can't be turned into capital.

recommendations.item: The Price of Onions
recommendations.creator: Ashok Desai
recommendations.context: Ajay brings it up at the start, when asked about the tomato price drama.
recommendations.reason: Tomatoes swinging between Rs 200 and Rs 2 a kg is the same story the book tells, with tomatoes in place of onions. India has been through this before.

recommendations.item: Why the Future Doesn't Need Us
recommendations.creator: Bill Joy
recommendations.context: Ajay cites this 2000 Wired essay while pushing back on Amit's GMO enthusiasm.
recommendations.reason: Joy worried about micro-machines, nanotechnology and DNA editing, and argued that everything we know about how messy software is applies to those fields too. Ajay uses it to make the case for treating gene editing with respect, neither banning it nor rushing it.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points listeners to it while discussing how MSPs pushed farmers from pulses to cereals.
recommendations.reason: The episode tells people to eat less cereal, while government MSPs subsidise cereals and so worsen India's diabetes epidemic.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Episode 6 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended to anyone who missed it, during the discussion of the price system.
recommendations.reason: It explains how prices carry information and incentives, changing the behaviour of both consumers and producers. That is the foundation for this episode's analysis of the tomato crisis.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: A companion to this episode's central claim that farmers are still denied the basic liberties city dwellers take for granted.

recommendations.item: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (Episode 1 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
recommendations.context: Amit's very first episode, which was about scale and corporatisation in agriculture.
recommendations.reason: His guests argued that small farmers are forced to master two skills, farming and entrepreneurship, when they might prefer to specialise in one, and that tiny holdings make scale impossible.

recommendations.item: Futures Markets in Agriculture (Episode 12 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Shashidhar
recommendations.context: Mentioned when discussing the absence of agricultural futures markets in India.
recommendations.reason: Amit once thought futures were arcane finance that didn't concern ordinary people. This conversation showed him they can be a powerful tool for removing a farmer's uncertainty.

recommendations.item: The Right to Property (Episode 26 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Cited during the discussion of the ban on selling farmland for non-agricultural use.
recommendations.reason: Rajagopalan explains at length what this restriction leads to: depressed land prices, land-use-change scams, and farmers who can't exit agriculture.

recommendations.item: Our FSI Problem (Episode 11 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Brought up while extending the idea of 'dead capital' to urban building restrictions.
recommendations.reason: The source of Tabarrok's line that Bombay reclaims the sea when it should be reclaiming the sky. FSI limits leave enormous value unused.

recommendations.item: India's Water Crisis (Episode 60 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vishwanath S (zenrainman)
recommendations.context: Cited in the Punjab rice and free electricity discussion.
recommendations.reason: It covers groundwater depletion in India, which is driven partly by bore wells and tube wells drawing excess water because of bad incentives.

recommendations.item: The State of Our Farmers (Episode 86 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
recommendations.context: Amit's only Hindi episode, recorded at a gathering of farmer leaders near Nashik.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'a masterpiece of illumination'. It is where he heard farmers state free-market ideas drawn from lived experience.

recommendations.item: India's Agriculture Crisis (Episode 140 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand
recommendations.context: Cited in the MSP discussion.
recommendations.reason: Barun Mitra pointed out that in one year, MSPs were promised for 24 commodities but actually paid for only six. That is the gap between the promise and reality of MSPs.

recommendations.item: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (Episode 211 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions his many agriculture episodes, 'including with Ajay'. This one is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: A deeper look at the farm bills, which would have kept APMCs but given farmers the choice to sell elsewhere.

recommendations.item: Farmers, Technology and Freedom of Choice: A Tale of Two Satyagrahas
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The column Amit says he will link for the BT cotton story.
recommendations.reason: The written version of the BT cotton satyagraha and what followed, including the adoption figures he cites.

recommendations.item: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: One of the articles 'by both of us that we will link to'.
recommendations.reason: A short written version of the episode's main thesis, that state overreach is at the root of farmers' misery.

recommendations.item: We Must Save Our Farmers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked among the agriculture articles, from Pragati.
recommendations.reason: More of Amit's written case for freeing Indian agriculture.

recommendations.item: Economic freedom in agriculture
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked among the hosts' agriculture articles.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's written case for the episode's conclusion that what is wrong is a lack of freedom, with the state blocking voluntary bargains.

recommendations.item: India: An agricultural trade powerhouse
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the episode's argument for international trade.
recommendations.reason: It supports Ajay's point that the global market is the biggest stabiliser of food prices, which India's on-off import and export bans undermine.

recommendations.item: What happened to global food prices?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It connects to the episode's example of wheat prices rising after the Ukraine war while India banned exports.
recommendations.reason: Background on global food price movements and why Indian farmers should be free to sell abroad when world prices rise.

recommendations.item: Climate change for practical people
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It relates to Ajay's argument about climate change, migration and land markets.
recommendations.reason: It sets out Ajay's view that the world will not hold back carbon dioxide emissions, so adaptation, including people moving away from badly affected regions, becomes essential.

recommendations.item: CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) data
recommendations.creator: CMIE
recommendations.context: Ajay uses it to question the standard claim that 50-60% of Indians depend on agriculture.
recommendations.reason: If you ask whether people primarily rely on agriculture for their income, CPHS data gives about 35%, which Ajay considers a truer picture than surveys that count anyone doing some farm work.

recommendations.item: Rhyme and Reason
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The archive of the weekly limericks Amit wrote for the Sunday Times of India, which came up after his opening limerick.
recommendations.reason: Amit says this probably made him the only professional limerick writer in the world. He wrote about a hundred before they got too political for the paper.

core_ideas.concept: The Price System Is a Rationing Mechanism
core_ideas.explanation: If 90 units of tomatoes arrive instead of 100, the price must rise until enough buyers walk away, whether by switching to puree, changing recipes or doing without. How far it has to rise depends on how flexible people are. Staples like wheat and rice, which people buy without watching the price, need huge price swings to close a small gap. Discretionary luxuries like avocados need only a small rise. This is not the market malfunctioning; it is how the market works.
core_ideas.quote: So the price system should be understood as a rationing mechanism.

core_ideas.concept: Samuelson's Cobweb Model and the Three Decisions
core_ideas.explanation: In Paul Samuelson's cobweb model, farmers look at today's high tomato price, all plant more, the price crashes, and they pull back, so the boom-and-bust repeats forever. The model only works if three decisions go wrong. Farmers must choose what to sow by looking backward, the inputs they invest must be fixed, and there must be no storage technology. In healthy markets, people look ahead, adjust their inputs and store produce, so the cycle doesn't happen. A swing from Rs 2 to Rs 200 is a peculiarly Indian problem, not a normal feature of food markets.
core_ideas.quote: So to get the cobweb model, which is indeed a dysfunctionality that you can see in the world, you got to get these three decisions going wrong.

core_ideas.concept: Four Mechanisms That Stabilise Food Markets
core_ideas.explanation: Food markets elsewhere are calm because of four mechanisms. (1) Futures markets show everyone the expected price at harvest, so even farmers who never trade can make better sowing decisions. (2) Storage: cold chains and also processing into paste, puree or dehydrated onions, which moves food from now into the future. (3) Domestic trade moves surplus from one state to a shortage in another. (4) International trade treats the world market as an effectively infinite buffer stock. India has hobbled all four. For example, the Forward Markets Commission was mostly a game of banning things, and moving commodity futures under SEBI hasn't changed much. Whenever prices rise, policymakers want to shoot the messenger.
core_ideas.quote: It's important to emphasize that I don't need to be a user of the futures market. The price that the speculators make on the futures market is a public good.

core_ideas.explanation: Farming means understanding the land up to the farm gate. Storage and speculation are a separate skill: forecasting shortages, sourcing cheaply and putting your own money at risk to carry goods into a future where releasing them pushes prices down. Ajay calls this God's own work. But Indian cinema turned it into the villainous 'hoarding', and laws like the Essential Commodities Act discourage the private storage that would smooth out tomato price swings.
core_ideas.quote: Just like the populists hate intellectuals, the populists hate speculators.

core_ideas.concept: Speculation as Insurance: The Once-a-Decade Windfall
core_ideas.explanation: Running storage is a dull business most years, but once in ten or twenty years prices spike and the operator makes 'like a bandit'. That windfall is what pays for the decades of standing ready, like an option or an insurance premium. When the state seizes the upside at exactly that moment, it destroys the incentive to build the capacity in the first place. The same logic applies to vaccine makers whose pandemic-time pricing the state crushed: why would anyone invest in that capacity next time?
core_ideas.quote: But that once in 10 years, once in 20 years, you make like a bandit. The profit of that time pays for being there year after year for decades.

core_ideas.explanation: Farmers are legally required to sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, which makes it a state-created monopsony (a single buyer, the opposite of a monopoly). A few traders there collect rent. In an old study Amit recalls, farmers got Rs 2 for tomatoes that consumers paid Rs 20 for. With competing middlemen it might be Rs 10 and Rs 12, leaving both farmer and consumer Rs 8 better off. This is a negative-sum game for everyone except the rent-seekers, captured in Sharad Joshi's lines: 'I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay so much that you die too.'
core_ideas.quote: The farmer was selling his tomatoes to the APMC for two rupees, the consumer was buying it for twenty rupees.

core_ideas.explanation: Sharad Joshi's term turns a common urban belief upside down. City people think farmers live off subsidies such as free electricity. But export bans, trade restrictions and controlled markets mean farmers routinely get less than the world price for what they grow. Added up, Joshi calculated, this comes to billions. In net terms farmers are paying, not being paid, and the money is simply wasted.
core_ideas.quote: Farmers are giving money to the state, or rather, it is just money being wasted. It is left on the table.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay credits the economist B.S. Minhas with persuading his generation to drop the image of the farmer as a fool. Farmers understand incentives and act on them as well as anyone. Policies built on the assumption that farmers can't choose wisely, such as forbidding them to sell outside the APMC or to plant BT cotton, are both wrong and condescending.
core_ideas.quote: Farmers are people, they're every bit as bright as you and me in understanding incentives and understanding choices.

core_ideas.concept: Trade Is Between Individuals, Not Nations
core_ideas.explanation: Nobody would stop a sale between Andheri and Bandra, or Bombay and Pune. Most people would agree a farmer in Maharashtra should be able to sell to someone in Tamil Nadu, even though the Indian state restricts it. Amit asks why it should be any different when the buyer is in Georgia, Azerbaijan or Arkansas. Thinking in terms of nation-states hides the fact that every trade is a voluntary deal between two people who both gain.
core_ideas.quote: It is individuals playing a positive sum game and both of them benefit.

core_ideas.concept: Farming Is a Business, and One or Two Acres Is Subscale
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay has changed his mind on this. On one or two acres a farm lacks technology and choices, and slips into near-feudal dependence on one local person who lends money, sells inputs and buys the crop. Farming should be treated as a business, with a P&L, a balance sheet and risks. The way out is consolidating land into 20-, 200- or 2,000-acre operations through leasing and land markets, not romanticised cooperatives. Being a 'landless labourer' should simply mean supplying labour in a labour market. As Amit puts it, asking every farmer to also be an entrepreneur is like asking every banker to own his own little bank. Let the arrangements evolve on their own, like Sikh farmers from Punjab who farm land in Madhya Pradesh and Ukraine.
core_ideas.quote: When you are a one-acre farm, two acre farm, you're fundamentally subscale.

core_ideas.concept: Land-Use Restrictions Create Dead Capital and Trap Farmers
core_ideas.explanation: Agricultural land can only be sold to another farmer for farming, so its price stays artificially low. Changing the land-use certificate can raise its value 40 times, which is why a common scam is to buy farmland through connections and get it reclassified. Real farmers can't exit at fair value and can't borrow against their land. Holdings shrink with each generation as land is divided among children, which feeds agitations for reservations among landowning communities like the Jats, Patidars and Marathas. This is Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital', and Amit sees the same thing in untitled slums, idle government land and FSI limits.
core_ideas.quote: So this is just one of the completely bizarre laws where you're telling a farmer that hey you own your farm. But hey, guess what, man? You don't really own your farm.

core_ideas.concept: Liquid Land Markets as Climate Adaptation
core_ideas.explanation: Through his work at XKDR Forum, Ajay has concluded that the world is not holding back carbon emissions, and that warming will hit hardest above the Vindhyas. A sensible response would be for households to sell their land and start new lives south of the Vindhyas, in farming or something else. That requires working land markets at both ends. Without them, families cling to land that climate change is slowly ruining.
core_ideas.quote: They'll hug the land, they'll stay with the land much longer while climate change grinds away destroying their livelihoods and messing with their lives.

core_ideas.explanation: As countries grow they move people out of agriculture and from villages to cities. India liberalised the rest of its economy in 1991 but left agriculture out. Apart from strong growth from 1991 to 2011, India's growth has been weak and modern-sector jobs have not appeared. The commonly quoted figure is that 50-60% of people depend on agriculture, which produces about 14% of GDP. Ajay notes that this depends on how survey questions are worded. Counting only those who primarily earn from agriculture gives about 35% (CMIE CPHS data), still eight to nine times the level in advanced economies. Small plots also block mechanisation, so more people are needed to work the same land.
core_ideas.quote: Structural transformation is the transition of a primitive country out of agriculture and from rural to urban.

core_ideas.concept: MSPs Distort What India Grows and Eats
core_ideas.explanation: Minimum support prices began with good intentions, but they skew incentives. When cereals got an MSP, farmers moved out of pulses, and for decades India grew too few pulses, the main source of protein for people who don't eat animals. That is an unseen nutritional cost. Cereals became the subsidised crop and pulses were left to the market, so the state ended up encouraging the very carbohydrates that drive India's diabetes epidemic. And as Barun Mitra found, MSPs promised for 24 commodities were actually paid for only six.
core_ideas.quote: And instead the government is subsidizing the cereal and amplifying the Indian diabetes epidemic.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit credits the agricultural economist Ashok Gulati with this shift in perspective. Rice and sugarcane are extremely water-intensive, and India exports both, so in effect India is one of the world's biggest exporters of water. It does this in a country with droughts and chronic shortages, because MSPs and free power make these crops artificially attractive.
core_ideas.quote: To think that we are actually one of the world's biggest exporters of water just blows my mind.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Hate the Middleman, Fix the Rules
core_ideas.explanation: Anger at the gap between the farm-gate price and the consumer price often turns into populist hatred of middlemen, who in India often belong to particular occupational castes or are rich. Ajay sees in this an old, Prussian-style love-of-the-land feeling. His warning is that individuals who make the most of the constraints they are given are not the villains. The fault lies with a state that stops voluntary bargains from solving the problem.
core_ideas.quote: Actually all that's going on here is a lack of freedom. That's all.

core_ideas.concept: GMOs: Settled Science vs. Respect for Complexity
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says GM crops are as close to scientific consensus as anything gets. Billions of meals have been eaten, BT brinjal is widely used in Bangladesh, golden rice helped children in the Philippines avoid blindness, and the precautionary principle taken too far stops all progress. He adds that opposition often comes from interested parties, such as the pesticide lobby and NGOs whose funding depends on alarm. Ajay takes a middle position: editing DNA is harder than editing code, and we know how badly code goes wrong. So we shouldn't ban gene editing, but we should approach it with caution.
core_ideas.quote: I think of editing DNA as being a wee bit harder than editing computer code.

core_ideas.concept: Bad Policy Is Downstream of Bad Ideas
core_ideas.explanation: India's agricultural controls did not come from nowhere. They came from the leading agricultural economics of an earlier generation. Echoing Keynes, Ajay argues that the bottleneck is knowledge. India needs a new generation of thinkers to build new ideas and research and change the climate of opinion, and policy will follow.
core_ideas.quote: What is wrong in India is the lack of ideas, is the lack of knowledge. And that is the choke point.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens with a limerick called 'Tomato' about Ajay blushing at YouTube praise: 'My good friend Ajay sat in his bed / reading YouTube comments in his head. / He was all aglow, like a tomato. / The fulsome praise made his cheeks go red.'

Ajay admits that as a 'callow immature youth' he produced a limerick every ten minutes, so the mathematician Meena Mahajan, a year senior at college, nicknamed him 'Limya' in the Maharashtrian style. Amit replies that he may be the world's only professional limerick writer, having written a weekly limerick for the Sunday Times of India until it got too political.

Ajay on the tomato price spike: people flying in from abroad were asked to fill the rest of their bags with tomatoes. Amit follows with: 'Are you hiding tomatoes in your cheeks or are you happy to see me?'

Ajay calls storage 'God's own work' and blames Bengalis: 'because there were so many Bengali movies around hoarders,' storage got a bad name and the state outlawed it. Amit, who is half Bengali, replies: 'For the purpose of this episode, Ajay, I'm half Punjabi. We shall not refer to the other half... there is plenty to blame us Punjabis also for, as we shall find out.' That sets up the later Punjab rice and stubble-burning story.
During the CPMC-for-columnists thought experiment, Amit tells Ajay: 'I hope you're the best paid columnist in India, but perhaps not.'

After Ajay's sobering point about climate change and frozen land markets, Amit offers what he calls 'probably an inappropriate joke': if the state won't let land markets be liquid, maybe climate change will.

Amit, on behalf of a viewer, sets Ajay a quota of at least one book recommendation per episode instead of masala tea. Ajay defends himself: 'books are very nerdy and I'm very nerdy. So I thought it'd be hazaar cool to go beyond books and talk about fun things like kefir and masala tea.' Amit closes the show: 'Books are hazaar cool.'

Sharad Joshi's couplet, spoken by a farmer to a consumer: 'Marte tum bhi ho, marte hum bhi hain.' Amit translates: 'I die my friend and so do you. I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay so much that you die too.'
Amit borrows the Hotel California line to describe farmers who can't sell their land at fair value: 'you can check out but you can never leave.'
Ajay invokes Keynes's warning about 'madmen' in power who are really following 'academic scribblers' of an earlier time, to argue that today's farm policies come from obsolete agricultural economics.
Alex Tabarrok on Mumbai's FSI limits, as Amit recalls it: 'in Bombay you reclaim the sea. You need to reclaim the sky.'

A shift in perspective Amit credits to Shruti Rajagopalan: the most common and most useful mass transit vehicle in the world is the elevator. We just don't count it as transport because it moves vertically.
